business_model: Direct-to-consumer digital renters and homeowners insurance carrier, app-driven claims/underwriting
anti_contamination_note: Cutoff frozen at 2017-12-19 (Series C announcement date) before evidence beyond 'a SoftBank-led round exists around Dec 2017' was gathered. The loss-ratio figure used below is drawn from a 2019-dated Forbes article that explicitly reports the value 'at the end of 2017' -- a fact-date-vs-report-date case handled the same way as Meetup's and Jawbone's evidence repairs in the original 15-company portfolio: the fact describes the snapshot period, the reporting date does not.

historical_evidence.company: Founded 2015, launched its first product (renters insurance) in New York in September 2016, a digital-first insurance carrier using an app-driven underwriting and claims process.
historical_evidence.market: Large, heavily regulated insurance market; renters/homeowners insurance specifically has historically low switching activity and low customer engagement, a real structural challenge for a new entrant regardless of product quality.
historical_evidence.team: No specific founder-background detail found in the primary source reviewed for this snapshot.
historical_evidence.product: App-based renters/homeowners insurance with a stated fast claims-processing/underwriting model, positioned as a modern alternative to traditional broker-sold policies.
historical_evidence.execution: Raised $120 million in a round announced December 19, 2017, led by SoftBank Group's Vision Fund, with GV (Alphabet), General Catalyst, and Sequoia Capital participating.
historical_evidence.traction: Disclosed 90,000 policyholders as of the snapshot date ('policies worth tens of billions of dollars' -- likely referring to aggregate insured/coverage value, not premium, and preserved verbatim rather than reinterpreted). Prior comparison point: approximately 16,000 policies sold in the first half of 2017 (roughly six months before the snapshot), sourced to secondary/aggregator reporting rather than independently re-verified against a primary outlet in this research pass, and treated with correspondingly lower confidence.
historical_evidence.financial: A loss ratio (claims paid divided by premiums collected) of 166% 'at the end of 2017' is reported by a 2019 Forbes article, explicitly describing the snapshot-period fact rather than a later period -- a real, quantified, dated, negative economics signal, with the source itself contextualizing it against a 65-70% range for large incumbent insurers as the healthy comparison point, and explicitly characterizing it as 'unsustainable.'

normalized_facts.source: Aggregated secondary reporting, not independently re-verified against a primary article in this research pass
Forbes (Jeff Kauflin, 'First, Fire All The Brokers...', published 2019-05-02, reporting a fact explicitly dated to end-of-2017)
normalized_facts.note: report-date postdates the snapshot by ~17 months, but the disclosed fact itself describes the end-of-2017 period -- same fact-date-vs-report-date reasoning used elsewhere in this benchmark program; the healthy-industry comparison figure (65-70%) is contemporaneous framing supplied by the same source, not a later retrospective judgment
